claims.text: Premelting and melting of solid Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu HEA nanoparticles are governed by kinetically limited atomic mobility in the solid precursor.
Dilution of each element in a five-component mixture suppresses rapid nucleation of segregated phases.
Suppressed segregation nucleation broadens the premelting and melting interval relative to binary or single-metal nanoparticles.
The initially solid HEA nanoparticles are prepared by low-temperature solid-state reduction of mixed-metal precursors.
The elements are initially distributed homogeneously within the nanoparticles.
Atomic mobility is limited in the initially solid nanoparticles.
Moderate heating rates under an inert atmosphere will keep atomic mobility restricted.
Particle size and shape should be matched across HEA, binary-alloy, and single-metal comparison groups.
Limited mobility and dilute constituent concentrations jointly hinder formation of distinct segregated phases during heating.
Restricted mobility and low local concentrations suppress sharp phase transitions in the HEA nanoparticles.
Slow local atomic rearrangements during heating produce a gradual transition and a broad melting range.
Simpler particle systems undergo more abrupt transitions because their higher local concentration of a given metal enables cooperative phase nucleation.
The HEA nanoparticles will exhibit a broadened melting onset in DSC and in-situ thermal observations.
The HEA nanoparticles will undergo a more gradual thermal transition than matched binary-alloy or single-metal nanoparticles.
Matched binary-alloy or single-metal nanoparticles will exhibit sharper, better-defined melting peaks.
Post-melt cooling will consolidate a uniform elemental distribution if kinetic limitations prevent segregation.
The proposed mechanism applies to nanoparticles produced by low-mobility solid-state methods and at sizes for which diffusion is sufficiently limited.
At high atomic mobility, such as during solution-phase synthesis or significantly slower cooling, other factors may dominate the transition behavior.
The transition width and temperature interval may depend on particle size, heating rate, and inter-element interactions.
Statistically indistinguishable melting onset and DSC peak sharpness between the HEA and matched simpler nanoparticles would falsify the proposed explanation.
